title: From Volleyball Courts to Rashtrapati Bhavan: Praveen Kumar's Padma Shri Crowns a Remarkable Journey
excerpt: The 22-year-old Paralympic gold medallist and world number one para high jumper will receive India's fourth-highest civilian honour on May 25, cementing the country's growing recognition of disability sport
body:
## The Highest Bar

On May 25, when Praveen Kumar walks into the Durbar Hall at Rashtrapati Bhavan to receive the Padma Shri from the President of India, the symbolism will be unmistakable. Here is a young man who has spent his athletic career clearing bars that others deemed impossible—and who now receives his country's formal acknowledgement that his achievements deserve a place alongside India's most distinguished citizens.

Praveen, just 22 years old and already a world number one in para high jump, will be honoured for his gold medal at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, where he cleared 2.08 metres in the men's T64 category to set a new Asian record. It was the culmination of a trajectory that has been, by any measure, extraordinary.

## A Boy from Noida

Born in 2003 in Noida, on the eastern fringe of Delhi's sprawl, Praveen came into the world with a congenital condition that left one leg shorter than the other. In a country where disability still carries a heavy social stigma, particularly in smaller towns and working-class families, his early years were defined by the quiet determination to be treated no differently from his peers.

The pivotal moment came in 2018, when coach Satyapal Singh spotted the 15-year-old playing volleyball at a local sports ground. Singh saw something in the teenager's explosive jumping ability and convinced him to try high jump. Within two years, Praveen was representing India at the highest level. At the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics—held in 2021—he won silver at just 18, announcing himself to the world.

## Paris and the Asian Record

The upgrade from silver to gold in Paris was no foregone conclusion. The T64 category, which includes athletes with below-knee limb deficiency or impairment, features fierce international competition. But Praveen arrived in the French capital as the form athlete, having dominated the world circuit in the preceding 18 months.

His clearance of 2.08 metres—an Asian record—was achieved with a composure that belied the occasion. To put the height in context, India's able-bodied national high jump record stands at 2.25 metres; Praveen's mark, achieved with a prosthetic running blade, is a testament to both his natural ability and the sophistication of modern para-athletics training.

He became only the second Indian to win Paralympic gold in high jump, following Mariyappan Thangavelu's triumph in Rio 2016. Together, they have established India as a genuine force in the discipline. Praveen's growing collection of honours—the Arjuna Award, the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, and now the Padma Shri—reflects the rapidly changing status of para-sport in Indian public life.

## Beyond Cricket: A Cultural Shift

Praveen's Padma Shri arrives at a moment of broader transformation in how India—and its diaspora—engage with sport beyond cricket. The Paris Paralympics saw India win 29 medals, its best-ever haul, generating unprecedented media coverage and public interest. Para-athletes who once competed in near-anonymity now enjoy sponsorship deals, social media followings, and invitations to the kind of ceremonial occasions that were once the exclusive preserve of cricketers and film stars.

The ceremony on May 25 will also honour Algoza maestro Taga Ram Bheel, a reminder that the Padma awards celebrate excellence across India's cultural spectrum. But it is the inclusion of para-athletes like Praveen that signals a subtle but significant shift in the nation's definition of sporting heroism.

## The Diaspora Connection

For the Indian diaspora, Praveen's story resonates on multiple levels. NRI communities, increasingly vocal in championing disability rights and inclusion, have embraced para-athletes as emblems of a more progressive India. His journey from a congenital condition to the summit of world sport embodies the Indian ethos of perseverance and self-improvement that diaspora families often cite as foundational values.

There is a practical dimension too. Indian sports fans abroad are diversifying their viewing habits. Where once the IPL and international cricket monopolised attention, Paris 2024 saw record streaming numbers for Paralympic events among NRI audiences. Praveen's generation of para-athletes is expanding the very definition of what it means to be an Indian sports fan—and the diaspora is leading that cultural shift.

## What Comes Next

At 22, Praveen's career is still in its early chapters. The Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics are three years away, and he has spoken publicly about his ambition to defend his title and push beyond the 2.10-metre barrier. With the Padma Shri secured, the national honours are largely accounted for. What remains is the prospect of further athletic greatness—and the continued elevation of Indian para-sport from the margins to the mainstream.

When he clears his next bar, whether at Rashtrapati Bhavan or in competition, it will carry the weight of a generation's aspirations.
